The paper received mixed but overall positive evaluations, with two accepts, one borderline accept, and one borderline reject. Reviewers highlighted several strengths, including the introduction of multi-view regularization, architectural improvements, and the curated FFHQC dataset (Reviewers #SFiD, #VAzj, #ymYL). The primary concerns were raised by Reviewer #QMop, who noted the absence of comparisons with diffusion-based approaches.

In the rebuttal, the authors clarified the instability issues arising from the removal of view-conditioning (#SFiD), explained identity consistency in 3DGS (#ymYL), outlined plans for clearer architectural comparisons (#SFiD), and defended the use of GANs as preferable for 3D generation under limited data availability (#VAzj, #ymYL). Both #VAzj and #SFiD were satisfied with these clarifications and upheld their support for acceptance. Reviewer #ymYL also endorsed acceptance after rebuttal, while Reviewer #QMop maintained that comparisons to diffusion models were necessary and therefore recommended borderline reject.

During the AC–reviewer discussion, Reviewers #VAzj and #ymYL emphasized that GANs are more appropriate under the current data constraints and argued that meaningful comparisons to diffusion-based models are not straightforward in this setting, countering #QMop’s concerns.

After weighing the reviews, rebuttal, and reviewer discussion, the AC aligns with the majority view. While Reviewer #QMop’s reservations are acknowledged, the paper received strong and consistent support from the other three reviewers. Accordingly, the AC recommends acceptance.

Dear Reviewers,

Thank you for your thorough evaluations and valuable feedback. We are pleased to see the overall positive reception of our work and are confident in addressing all identified weaknesses and suggestions for improvement prior to the camera-ready deadline.

Specifically, we will make the following updates to the manuscript and supplementary materials:

1. Clarify that the instability arises from the removal of view-conditioning (SFiD Q2).
2. Add a supplementary figure comparing our generator architecture to that of GSGAN (SFiD Weakness 2).
3. Improve the explanation of the view-conditioning concept (QMop Weakness 1).
4. Elaborate on why GANs are a suitable choice over diffusion models for synthesizing 3D content from 2D data (QMop Weakness 2).
5. Include additional ablation studies in the supplementary materials (QMop Weakness 3).
6. Emphasize that while the data curation process improves visual quality, it is not strictly required for stable training (VAzj Weakness 1).

We sincerely appreciate your time, effort, and constructive input.

Best regards,

The Authors

Dear Reviewer VAzj,

Thank you for your positive review. In the following we will go through the weaknesses and questions.

_**Weakness 1:** Fig. 6 (left) shows that model can still predict 3d "inconsistent" results, by volumetric-cheating. While the smile rebalancing helped in this scenario. It raises questions about the scalability of the method., e.g. whenever going to a new dataset one might have to go through tedious dataset curation._

Yes, that is true. Every time we deal with view-dependent biases like smiling or eye gaze, it is difficult to model those biases with a single static 3DGS scene. In such a case the model will likely apply volumetric-cheating to some degree. While re-balancing is one simple solution, we could alternatively forward the gaze or smiling information as a separate conditioning into the training pipeline. This way, the volumetric-cheating should also be reduced, while we would also be able to control those attributes during inference. While this might not be as applicable for other domains like cars or cats, those datasets probably possess little to no view-dependent biases, compared to human datasets.

---

_**Weakness 2:** It remains to be seen whether the proposed improvements also carry over to different datasets, and whether it can be scaled to larger image collection of faces without extreme data curation overhead until a good balance can be obtained._

That is definitely a direction that we want to go into. In our experiments, we see that the generator starts to outperform the discriminator at some point during the training. This possibly suggests that we can increase the complexity of the discriminator or the complexity of the training data even further. And although the data curation for FFHQ was very complex and contained a lot of manual filtering, we can now utilize the resulting dataset to automatically filter new images. 

---

_**Question 1:** The paper is focused on generating 3D heads, which is so far also the most important application of 3D GANs. Have the authors experiment with different datasets? Ultimately, one of the main things that is holding (3D) GANs back is the balance during training, and the authors claim to improve training stability. Ultimately, demonstrating more results on other datasets would solidify this claim and show the public that 3D GAN training is more accessible now._

For now, we have only experimented with face datasets, as they align well with our research. However, benchmarking our model across other datasets would be very interesting. For AFHQ and ShapeNet Cars it should be a straight forward adaption. For other datasets, good camera poses might be difficult to obtain, which are currently essential for the training pipeline. 

---

_**Question 2:* Similarly, I am wondering about the scalability w.r.t. to training data. It sounds like well balanced training data is especially important for GANs. How much effort would it be train the proposed model on large-scale dataset such as the LAION-Face subset? How much effort would go into data cleaning? Is there a clear recipe for the cleaning process, or is it a trial-and-error process that alternates between cleaning and training?_

We really like the idea to scale the model to larger datasets like LAION-Face. Given that the model also performed very well on the original FFHQ dataset, which included a lot of bad training samples, it might not even be required to go through such careful data pre-processing to achieve good results. The main reason to filter the dataset was to achieve results of higher quality rather than improving the stability. Additionally, since we now defined a set of good and bad training samples, we should be able to automate the filtering process. And even if we filtered out 70% of the 20 million images, we would still end up with 120 times more images than in FFHQC.

---

_**Question 3:** Fig. 6 (left) shows that without smiling rebalancing, the model can still generate a 3DGS point cloud, which appears to be 3D inconsistent. How can this be explained? Simply through volumetric cheating?_

Yes, the same can sometimes be observed with the eye gaze. The model aligns the Gaussian primitives in a way so that they are only visible from certain viewing angles, similarly to lenticular printing.

Dear Reviewer QMop,

Thank you for your review. In the following we will address the stated weaknesses and questions:

_**Question 1:** “Please refer to Strengths and Weaknesses”_

_**Weakness 1.** “The motivation of the article is not clearly stated. In particular, don’t have a clear explanation of view-conditioning and camera pose, which makes the central claim—namely, that “without relying on view-conditioning”—difficult to follow.”_

We appreciate the reviewer’s feedback that our discussion of view-conditioning and camera pose was not sufficiently explicit. This is a very central component of the paper and understanding it is essential for understanding our main contribution. We will improve the text in the paper for better clarity. 
Below we offer a more intuitive explanation of view-conditioning to make sure that the concept is clear during the rebuttal dialog:

The general goal of generative 3D models is to produce a 3D scene (in our case a 3D head) that can be rendered from arbitrary views and used in 3D environments such as game engines or VR environments. This requires a 3D representation that looks realistically from any viewpoint without re-synthesizing it for each view. With current 3DGS GANs (GGHead and GSGAN) this is not possible due to the used view-conditioning. 
Since the introduction of the StyleGAN architecture, most GANs (including all GANs discussed in the paper) are equipped with a mapping network that projects the random latent vector Z, sampled from a normal distribution, to a learned latent space W before forwarding it to the synthesis component of the generator. When using view-conditioning, the camera information is provided to this mapping network as well. If we now tell the generator to produce a 3D head, viewed from the left side, it can simply map the random latent vector towards a region in the learned latent space that renders the left side of the head especially well. While this produces good renderings for that specific view, the resulting 3DGS scene looks very poor when viewed in a 3D environment from novel views. 
Essentially, with view conditioning, the camera information is forwarded to the generator twice. First when mapping the latent vector and second  when rendering the 3DGS scene. If these cameras match, the quality is high. If they are different, quality drops as  shown in Figure 3. In our paper, we remove the first camera information that is forwarded to the mapping network but keep the camera information when rendering the 3DGS scene. Intuitively, the generator now does not know from which direction the scene will be rendered. Therefore, it has to create a head that looks realistically from any viewpoint.

In summary: Using view-conditioning allows the generator to ‘cheat’ as it already knows before the synthesis, from which angle the head will be rendered. This causes the generator to produce renderings that exclusively look good from that specific view. To produce good quality for any view, we would have to re-synthesize the scene each time we change the camera view. While this does not allow us to export the head as a single consistent 3D scene with high quality for any view, it also causes the identity to shift each time we re-synthesize the scene.

_“For example, if the camera view not included as training input, when rendering, how to indicate camera direction”_

Camera direction is still provided to the renderer during both training and inference.  What changes is that it is not used as an explicit conditioning signal inside the generator or its mapping network. This is precisely what we mean by training “without relying on view-conditioning.” We will incorporate this explanation into the paper for greater clarity.

_“And the rationale behind the experimental design in Figure 3 is likewise unclear: in what situation when utilizing GSGAN and GGHead will has the view-conditioning does not align with the camera pose, if this is a common phenomenon, or manually situation”,_ 

When using the synthesized 3DGS scenes of the generator and displaying it in a web browser, a game engine or a VR setting, we cannot re-synthesize the head each time so that the view-conditioning matches the current rendering view. Instead we require a fixed and consistent 3D scene that looks good from any viewpoint.

_“and why don’t have results of CGS-GAN itself in Figure 3.”_

We did not include our result in Figure 3 as it was intended to highlight the limitation of existing methods rather than providing a comparison. Such a comparison can be found in Figure 5, which essentially demonstrates the same observation with more examples. Nevertheless, if including our results in Figure 3 improves the overall clarity, we are happy to include it as well.

---

_**Weakness 2.** “All comparative evaluations are confined to GAN-based Gaussian-splatting methods (e.g., GSGAN, GGHead). Although earlier GAN-based methods demonstrate that 3D Gaussian-splatting can be realized within a GAN framework, but the paper does not conduct a systematic comparison with state-of-the-art diffusion approaches (e.g., Morphable Diffusion, Gaussian3Diff, etc.). Consequently, it leaves unanswered (i) how CGS-GAN fares in image fidelity, 3D consistency, and computational efficiency relative to diffusion-based generators, and (ii) why a GAN architecture is still preferable—or at least competitive—in an era where diffusion models dominate high-quality generative synthesis.”_

Although in recent years diffusion-based approaches have surpassed the rendering quality of GANs for some domains (2D synthesis or video generation), GANs still stand out for their efficient real-time editing and rendering capabilities and their clear advantage to not require 3D ground-truth data. The latter is especially important for 3D synthesis, as real 3D ground truth data is very difficult to obtain. This also goes for the two mentioned models GAUSSIAN3DIFF and Morphable Diffusion. GAUSSIAN3DIFF uses a pre-trained 3D-aware GAN (PanoHead) to create 3D ground truth data, and Morphable Diffusion creates pseudo 3D ground truth data using Zero-1-to-3 and SyncDreamer. 
In contrast, 3D GANs can be trained on a large collection of 2D images, without requiring multiview information. Additionally, instead of overfitting the 3D scene to a single given person like in Morphable Diffusion or Diffusion Avatars, which can be very time consuming and computationally expensive using a diffusion model, GANs create a latent space with unlimited identities that each can be synthesized in less than 0.01 seconds.
For all those reasons, we treat 3D GANs and diffusion methods as two separate classes of models and do not make comparisons between them. 

---

_**Weakness 3.** “Limited ablation analysis. The paper does not disentangle the contributions of the architectural choices, multi-view regularization, and modified conditional loss from the baseline with clear ablation. A more granular ablation would clarify which components are responsible for the observed performance gains.“_

In the paper, we provide some ablations for the most important components. This includes the visual comparisons in Figure 6, where we deactivate the smile rebalancing, compare the cropping strategies and the random background augmentation. Additionally, we provide a small ablation in the text (starting from line 309) for the multiview-regularization, where we argue that rendering four times is ideal. This was not supported with numbers in the submitted version, but we are going to add the numbers in the supplementary material.

---

_**Weakness 4.**. “Generally, the paper is incremental work based on GSGAN, cannot extract clear motivation and sufficient novelty, and also cannot see obvious improvement in experiments.”_

In the following, we list our contributions, which we believe are novel and clearly improve state-of-the-art methods:
Proper 3D consistent output scenes without relying on view-conditioning as prior methods
Significantly higher output resolutions compared to prior methods of up to 2048
- A lightweight generator architecture with reduced memory footprint and faster synthesis speed
- A new metric (FID_3D) for evaluating the quality of 3D scenes rather than 2D generated images
- Improved FID and FID_3D results compared to prior methods
- A random background augmentation for reducing the hole artifacts
- A multi-view regularization that stabilizes the training convergence
- Revised conditional loss function for better training stability
- A high quality dataset FFHQC with:
     - resolutions of up to 2048x2048
     - removed training samples that harm the quality
     - a re-cropping strategy for synthesizing the entire head
     - a smile rebalancing for reducing view-dependent biases

---

_**Question 2.** “In the Figure 5 visualization, why do you use different identities for different methods? The same source images should be used for testing different methods.”_

We understand the reviewer’s concern and would like to explain why showing exactly the same face across methods is not feasible. The identity of the rendered faces of 3D GANs is not controllable. This is because each model learns its own latent space that can be completely different. A latent vector that encodes one identity in CGS-GAN has no semantic meaning in GSGAN or GGHead. In Figure 5, we aimed to choose fair comparisons that best represented the strengths and weaknesses for each model. The main takeaway message from Figure 5 is that both prior methods either change the identity when re-synthesizing the heads with the current view conditioning, or produce very poor renderings when fixing the view-conditioning.

---

rebuttal.value:
Dear Reviewer SFiD,

Thank you for your thorough review and the overall positive rating. We aim to improve the clarity of the paper by addressing the following questions and weaknesses:

_**Q1: Generalizability:**
“How well does the CGS-GAN framework perform when applied to 3D synthesis of objects other than human heads?“_

In prior works, GSGAN or EG3D showed that 3D GANs generalize well for other domains such as cats (AFHQv2 Dataset) or cars (ShapeNet Cars Dataset). Therefore, we expect  CGS GAN to handle these datasets successfully, potentially with less difficulty as cat and car images exhibit fewer view-dependent biases and dynamic expressions. By contrast, human datasets are challenging as subjects often gaze directly towards the camera lens and are more likely to smile, creating strong pose- and expression-related correlations.
For the present work, we focused on human heads, as this application is widely relevant, while it also aligns well with our future research ideas.


_“Are there plans to extend this method to more general 3D object generation?”_

Extending the method for more general object generation would be a very interesting addition to the method, but is currently not our focus. However, we will publish the code so that this can be done in future work.

---

_**Q2: Training Stability:** The authors mention that without multi-view regularization, the model tend to collapse after 8M training steps, but GSGAN seem not to have this kind of regularization. Does this unstability introduced by the difference of upsampling operations?_

The instability is introduced by removing the view-conditioning. In GSGAN, the generator always receives the viewing direction, allowing it to ‘cheat’: it can synthesize heads that look good only from that defined direction but poorly from any other direction. This is no longer the case with our method, which learns to synthesize 3D consistent heads whose appearance is plausible and consistent from any viewpoint. This training objective with multi-view consistency is much more challenging and causes the training to be less stable.

---

_**A minor question:** “In the supplementary material, the authors mentioned that they use a cube with side legth of 1(like EG3D) instead of 2, does this choice significantly influence the training process or the final performance?”_

Using the same settings as in EG3D (side length of 1m, a radius of 2.7m and a FoV of 12°) makes sense as it aligns well with the average camera settings from the real images in the training dataset. However, as these values are very rough estimations, it does not make a big difference for the training performance when using different settings as in GSGAN (side length of 2m, a radius of 2.7m and a FoV of ~20°). It is, however, important to scale all Gaussian primitives accordingly and adapt the regularizations from GSGAN that enforce clustering and penalize if Gaussian primitives move too far from the center.

---

_**Weakness 1:** “Scope: A potential limitation is the focus on human head synthesis, which may restrict the method's applicability to other 3D objects, for example AFHQ, where the pre-proecess procedure might not be available.”_

The pre-processing steps that were done to create FFHQC include a semi-manual filtering of bad images, re-cropping, background masking, smile rebalancing and pose rebalancing. All of those steps, apart from the smile rebalancing, can be applied to new datasets (like AFHQ or ShapeNet Cars) as well. If the new dataset introduces new view-dependent biases it might cause some inconsistencies. Those can either be addressed by resampling or ignored, as the model will still produce good results.

_**Weakness 2** “Unclear Presentation: The distinction between the proposed generator architecture and that of GSGAN is not clearly articulated in the paper. While the authors do describe some detailed differences in the text, such as the variation in the upsample operation, I would suggest including a dedicated figure to visually highlight the core differences between the two. Furthermore, the textual description should also be revised to more prominently emphasize these key distinctions.”_

Thank you for this valuable comment.  Due to limited space in the main paper, we will add such a comparison figure to the supplementary materials.

Dear Reviewer ymYL,

Thank you for your very positive review. In the following, we will address your questions and concerns wrt potential weaknesses.

_**Weakness 1:** The claim that removing camera conditioning typically destabilizes training—even leading to collapse—may be overstated. In my experience, 3D GANs can still be trained stably without camera conditioning. However, doing so often leads to identity inconsistency during inference: when rendering from different viewpoints with a fixed latent code w, the identity of the generated face may shift. One benefit of camera conditioning is that by fixing it (e.g., to a frontal view) during inference, the identity can remain consistent across viewpoints. I may be missing some insight here, and I would welcome further discussion or clarification on this point._

In our own experiments, removing view conditioning from GSGAN and GGHead led to very poor performance. Especially in early training stages, the generator fails to  keep up with the discriminator, leading to either (i) full collapse (GSGAN) or to (ii) significantly slower and less stable convergence (GGHead). Regarding the remark on identity inconsistency, we did not observe identity changes in any of our results, with and without view-conditioning. We assume that  identity inconsistency is more pronounced in NeRF based 3D GANs, given they are less constrained to produce discrete 3D scenes.

---

_**Weakness 2:** The authors claim that their generator can be trained without camera conditioning while still producing consistent 3D heads from any viewpoint. However, it is unclear how identity consistency is maintained during inference when the camera viewpoint changes. In previous works, removing camera conditioning often led to identity drift across views. Could the authors clarify which component(s) of their approach—such as the improved 3DGS generator architecture or multi-view regularization—specifically contribute to preserving identity consistency in the absence of camera conditioning?_

We did not observe identity changes when disabling the view-conditioning for GSGAN and GGHead or our approach. This is likely due to the nature of 3DGS, which might make it very difficult to model inconsistent identities with discrete point clouds.

---

_**Question 1:** The paper proposes averaging gradients from multiple rendered views per training step to improve stability, but it's unclear how this averaging is implemented. Are the gradients from different views treated equally?_

The implementation of gradient averaging is very simple. In pytorch, we compute a loss and then apply the gradient with the backward() function:

```py
loss = -softplus(-D(G(latent, view)))
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
```

If we now accumulate the loss across a larger sample size before calling the backward function, we can average the gradients.

```py
loss  = softplus(-D(G(latent, view_1)))
loss += softplus(-D(G(latent, view_2)))
loss += softplus(-D(G(latent, view_3)))
loss += softplus(-D(G(latent, view_4)))
loss /= 4
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
```

This way, each angle is treated equally.

---

_**Question2:** Is it possible to add a user study for comparative analysis?_

We agree that a user study is the best way to validate and compare the performance of 3D face generators. Due to limited time and resources, we had to rely on the well established FID metric and our proposed FID_3D metric. While purely computational, these correlate strongly with human preference. However, for future work, such a user study will probably be very interesting and could give valuable insights on how to improve such models even further.

The authors also developed a scalable generator capable of producing images at up to 2048x2048 resolution and created a new dataset, FFHQC, derived from FFHQ, with enhancements like larger head crops and filtered occluded images to improve side views. The framework achieves competitive FID scores, indicating high rendering quality, and addresses issues like hole artifacts through background augmentation.

**Strengths**:

**High Conceptual Novelty**: The primary strength is the explicit and architecturally enforced disentanglement of geometry and semantics. This is a more principled approach to controllable and 3D consistent generation and addresses a clear limitation of previous models. **Dataset Bias**: It proposes a simple and effective filtering method to rebalance the FFHQC dataset, reducing view-dependent effects and improving side view quality. This approach is not only effective for this work but also provides valuable techniques for other GAN research.

**Hole Artifacts**: It introduces random background augmentation to mitigate "hole artifacts" in generated images, enhancing rendering quality and training stability, which can benefit other GAN applications.

summary.value: CGS-GAN is a 3D Gaussian-splatting GAN framework that enables stable training and high-quality 3D-consistent synthesis of human heads without relying on view-conditioning, it can synthesizes high-resolution (up to 2048²) human heads that remain identity-consistent through multi-view regularization and conditional loss. In addition, the work introduces FFHQ-Clean, a re-cropped, de-occluded, pose- and expression-balanced extension of FFHQ designed to mitigate floating artifacts, occlusions, and smile bias. Experiments show that CGS-GAN matches or surpasses GGHead and GSGAN across FID, FID-3D, and inference speed, while substantially lowering GPU memory usage and training time.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths: 
1.	The paper is well-written and easy to understand.
2.	Improves over GAN-based state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods.

Weaknesses:
1.	The motivation of the article is not clearly stated. In particular, don’t have a clear explanation of view-conditioning and camera pose, which makes the central claim—namely, that “without relying on view-conditioning”—difficult to follow. For example, if the camera view not included as training input, when rendering, how to indicate camera direction; And the rationale behind the experimental design in Figure 3 is likewise unclear: in what situation when utilizing GSGAN and GGHead will has the view-conditioning does not align with the camera pose, if this is a common phenomenon, or manually situation, and why don’t have results of CGS-GAN itself in Figure 3.
2.	All comparative evaluations are confined to GAN-based Gaussian-splatting methods (e.g., GSGAN, GGHead). Although earlier GAN-based methods demonstrate that 3D Gaussian-splatting can be realized within a GAN framework, but the paper does not conduct a systematic comparison with state-of-the-art diffusion approaches (e.g., Morphable Diffusion, Gaussian3Diff, etc.). Consequently, it leaves unanswered (i) how CGS-GAN fares in image fidelity, 3D consistency, and computational efficiency relative to diffusion-based generators, and (ii) why a GAN architecture is still preferable—or at least competitive—in an era where diffusion models dominate high-quality generative synthesis.
3.	Limited ablation analysis. The paper does not disentangle the contributions of the architectural choices, multi-view regularization, and modified conditional loss from the baseline with clear ablation. A more granular ablation would clarify which components are responsible for the observed performance gains.
4.	Generally, the paper is incremental work based on GSGAN, cannot extract clear motivation and sufficient novelty, and also cannot see obvious improvement in experiments.

final_justification.value:
I agree with Reviewer VAzj and the authors’ observation that 3D-GANs have the advantage of not requiring multi-view image observations of the same object. However, it is worth noting that there now exist several sizeable 3D head datasets—both real (e.g., RenderMe360) and synthetic (e.g., Head360)—that can be leveraged for training diffusion-based models. With appropriate priors, datasets containing hundreds or thousands of identities can be sufficient to achieve strong performance.

Because diffusion-based models require multi-view supervision, they can offer fine control over generated content using text prompts or single-image guidance. Recent works such as Portrait3D and DiffPortrait360 (both with publicly available code), as well as Morphable Diffusion (which should perform well when trained on RenderMe360), demonstrate this capability. In the literature, diffusion-based methods often compare with 3D-GANs on the image-to-3D task through GAN inversion techniques. This provides a straightforward and balanced way to make comparisons—by evaluating both approaches on the same input images (potentially with varied poses) and checking whether identity is preserved. Such an approach would also allow a fairer comparison with other 3D-GAN methods, avoiding selective emphasis on only ‘the strengths and weaknesses for each model’.

I would not suggest that unconditional generation from a random latent vector is less useful; maintaining an open mind about diverse generation paradigms is important. Nevertheless, given the availability of these datasets and methods, a controlled comparison—starting with the simplest case of single-image-to-3D generation—would be highly informative. This evaluation protocol has been adopted by other 3D-GAN works such as EG3D, PanoHead, and GSGAN, and it would be important to see how performs under the same setting against a diffusion-based baseline.

summary.value:
The paper improves 3D GAN frameworks, which are trained on large 2D datasets, with a special focus on 3D consistent generations and high-resolution results.

The paper claims that one of the main drawbacks of 3D GANs is the camera conditioning of the Generator, which is necessary in previous frameworks in order to keep a healthy balance between generator and discriminator. In order to remove this conditioning the paper introduces a multi-view regularization technique, where one generated 3D scene is rendered multiple times and gradients are averaged. After carefully accounting for batch statistics the authors show that this technique results in more 3d consistent generations. Furthermore, that authors improve the architecture from GSGAN, and make it more scalable to obtain more Gaussians. Using random background augmentation, the authors deny the Generator to exploit white background for modeling specular highlights, which results in holes in the predicted geometry.

Next to improving the network architecture and training scheme, the authors propose a careful data cleaning scheme and demonstrate that less, but more curated data results in better generations. Specifically, occluders are removed, frontal non-smiling images are added for better balance, and extreme view-point images are duplicated to balance the camera distribution. The new dataset is qualitatively shown to result in more consistent generations

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths**:
- Multi-view regularization allows for removal of camera conditioning in generator which finally makes 3D-aware GANS to actual 3D GANs. This is an important step for 3D generative that are trained merely on 2D image collections.
- The carefully designed dataset curation strategy significantly helps with generation quality.
- More smaller improvements such as generator architecture and random background colors lead to additional improvements.
- The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
- Thorough experiments validated the proposed ideas. The effects on training and rendering speed are also measured.

**Weakness**:
- Fig. 6 (left) shows that model can still predict 3d "inconsistent" results, by volumetric-cheating. While the smile rebalancing helped in this scenario. It raises questions about the scalability of the method., e.g. whenever going to a new dataset one might have to go through tedious dataset curation. 
- It remains to be seen whether the proposed improvements also carry over to different datasets, and whether it can be scaled to larger image collection of faces without extreme data curation overhead until a good balance can be obtained.


Overall, the paper shows careful considerations of many existing issues in 3D GANs (specially 3DGS-based 3D GANs). While some ideas might sound incremental, overall they accumulate to significant progress. The removal of the camera conditioning in the generator is of special importance, and has to potential to make 3D GANs more popular again in the future.

questions.value:
As the experimental section already presents thorough comparisons, there are not many important remaining questions that I can think of.

- The paper is focused on generating 3D heads, which is so far also the most important application of 3D GANs. Have the authors experiment with different datasets? Ultimately, one of the main things that is holding (3D) GANs back is the balance during training, and the authors claim to improve training stability. Ultimately, demonstrating more results on other datasets would solidify this claim and show the public that 3D GAN training is more accessible now. 
- Similarly, I am wondering about the scalability w.r.t. to training data. It sounds like well balanced training data is especially important for GANs. How much effort would it be train the proposed model on large-scale dataset such as the LAION-Face subset? How much effort would go into data cleaning? Is there a clear recipe for the cleaning process, or is it a trial-and-error process that alternates between cleaning and training?
- Fig. 6 (left) shows that without smiling rebalancing, the model can still generate a 3DGS point cloud, which appears to be 3D inconsistent. How can this be explained? Simply through volumetric cheating?

I stand by my original judgment, and vote for acceptance. 
The paper proposes several improvements for an already elaborate 3D-GAN system, especially the removal of camera conditioning in the generator is an important step for 3D-GANs.

3D-GANs, while it is not clear yet how well they can scale, are still a highly relevant research topic, due to their ability to learn 3D data distributions merely from a collection of 2D images with associated camera information.

title.value: CGS-GAN: 3D Consistent Gaussian Splatting GANs for High Resolution Human Head Synthesis

TLDR.value: We propose a new 3D Gaussian splatting GAN for 3D consistent rendering at high resolution

abstract.value: Recently, 3D GANs based on 3D Gaussian splatting have been proposed for high quality synthesis of human heads. However, existing methods stabilize training and enhance rendering quality from steep viewpoints by conditioning the random latent vector on the current camera position. This compromises 3D consistency, as we observe significant identity changes when re-synthesizing the 3D head with each camera shift. Conversely, fixing the camera to a single viewpoint yields high-quality renderings for that perspective but results in poor performance for novel views. Removing view-conditioning typically destabilizes GAN training, often causing the training to collapse. In response to these challenges, we introduce CGS-GAN, a novel 3D Gaussian Splatting GAN framework that enables stable training and high-quality 3D-consistent synthesis of human heads without relying on view-conditioning. To ensure training stability, we introduce a multi-view regularization technique that enhances generator convergence with minimal computational overhead. Additionally, we adapt the conditional loss used in existing 3D Gaussian splatting GANs and propose a generator architecture designed to not only stabilize training but also facilitate efficient rendering and straightforward scaling, enabling output resolutions up to $2048^2$. To evaluate the capabilities of CGS-GAN, we curate a new dataset derived from FFHQ. This dataset enables very high resolutions, focuses on larger portions of the human head, reduces view-dependent artifacts for improved 3D consistency, and excludes images where subjects are obscured by hands or other objects. As a result, our approach achieves very high rendering quality, supported by competitive FID scores, while ensuring consistent 3D scene generation.

abstract.description: Abstract of paper. Add TeX formulas using the following formats: $In-line Formula$ or $$Block Formula$$.

pdf.description: Upload your submission as a PDF file that ends with .pdf. In this file the main text (max. nine pages), references, and checklist may be followed by technical appendices, for which there is no page limit. Paper PDF can be updated until the full paper submission deadline (May 15)

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

enum.description: I confirm that I have included a paper checklist in the paper PDF.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and ensure all material is anonymized. The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22)

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/ ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**

enum.description: We acknowledge the responsible reviewing obligations as authors.

LLM_usage.description: This checklist collects statistical information on how NeurIPS authors use Generative AI (e.g., LLMs) in manuscript preparation. Responses are confidential and will not be shared with reviewers, area chairs, or senior chairs. The PC Chairs will analyze aggregated data to understand how emerging technologies influence the research publication process. Please select all that apply below.
